standard.title: Locate, select and compare information
standard.description: locate, select and compare information, data and ideas from a range of sources
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have located, selected and compared information from a range of sources at Year 9 (AC9HC9S02). They can use digital tools to survey political issues and explore media for bias and representation.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students locate, select and compare information, data and ideas from a range of sources about political, legal or civic issues, evaluating sources for credibility, perspective and relevance.

nodes.label: Locating relevant sources across a range
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can locate print and online sources relevant to a political, legal or civic issue, selecting sources that represent varying and conflicting points of view.
nodes.minimum_width: Locate at least three sources on a civic issue that represent at least two different perspectives, including at least one print or formal source and one digital source.
nodes.typical_width: Locate print and online sources that represent varying and conflicting points of view on a contemporary political, legal or civic issue, including traditional media, social media, government documents, and survey/polling data.
wider: Use digital survey or polling tools to collect primary data on a political issue and evaluate how survey design affects the results obtained
Investigate how different media environments (traditional vs social media) make particular types of civic information more or less visible or accessible
Locate sources produced by groups whose perspectives are typically underrepresented in mainstream civic debate and evaluate what they add to the issue
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who locate only one perspective or who cannot deliberately seek out conflicting views will produce incomplete analysis — the comparison and evaluation in subsequent nodes depends on having sources that represent genuine variation.

response_modes.reason: Teach source-mapping as a deliberate strategy — students should plan their source search to ensure perspective diversity, not just gather whatever appears first. Model the difference between varied and echo-chamber sourcing.

success_criteria: Locates at least three sources relevant to the civic issue
Sources represent at least two different perspectives or points of view
Includes both print/formal and digital sources

nodes.label: Evaluating sources for credibility and bias
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate sources for credibility, perspective and potential bias, including identifying stereotypes, over-generalisation and misrepresentation in media.
nodes.minimum_width: Evaluate at least two sources for credibility and perspective, identifying one potential bias or limitation in each.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate sources for credibility, perspective and potential bias — including examining traditional and social media texts for stereotypes, over-generalisation and misrepresentation, such as those related to how cultural groups or immigrants are represented.
wider: Conduct a detailed media analysis comparing how two different outlets frame the same civic issue, identifying specific language choices and representation patterns
Investigate how algorithms shape what civic information different users see on social media and evaluate what this means for an informed citizenry
Compare the policies of different political groups on a contested issue and evaluate the framing choices each group makes in presenting their position

response_modes.reason: Source evaluation requires explicit criteria. Students benefit from a structured framework (e.g. authority, accuracy, purpose, perspective) rather than general scepticism — teach the evaluative categories before applying them to specific sources.

The algorithm and social media direction gives students a systemic rather than individual-source view of bias — understanding how information environments are structured is a different and richer analytical move.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The algorithmic information environment direction is substantively distinct from individual source evaluation — it raises the question of structural rather than incidental bias, which is a qualitatively different analytical capability.
success_criteria: Evaluates at least two sources for credibility and perspective
Identifies a specific potential bias or limitation in at least one source
Distinguishes between a source's viewpoint and factual error

nodes.label: Selecting and comparing across sources
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can select relevant information from multiple sources and compare them to identify patterns, conflicts and gaps in the civic evidence base.
nodes.minimum_width: Select information from at least three sources and compare them, identifying at least one point of agreement and one point of conflict.
nodes.typical_width: Select varying and conflicting information across sources and compare them systematically, identifying points of agreement, conflict and significant gaps — and explaining what these patterns reveal about the civic issue being investigated.
wider: Compare the information available on a civic issue from Australian government sources versus international bodies (e.g. UN reports) and evaluate what each source can and cannot tell you
Investigate a civic issue where survey data and media representation conflict and analyse what explains the difference
Extend source comparison to include perspectives from First Nations Australians or communities directly affected by the issue and evaluate what their perspectives add

response_modes.reason: This node integrates source location and evaluation into comparative analysis — students must synthesise across multiple sources rather than treating each individually. Teaching investment is in supporting the move from 'source A says X, source B says Y' to 'these sources conflict because...'.

success_criteria: Selects information from at least three sources
Identifies at least one point of agreement and one point of conflict across sources
Explains what the pattern of agreement and conflict reveals about the issue
